## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
According to its opening frame narrative, the Buddha recounted the story while residing at Jetavana with reference to a certain monk who lived in a forest near a border village in the Kosala country after receiving meditation instructions from the Master [SuttaCentral]. The past narrative concerns the virtue of frugality and features an exchange between Sakka and the parrot [Burlingame 1921].
In discussing the Dhammapada Commentary's version of the story of Tissa of the market-town, Eugene W. Burlingame notes that the commentary has Sakka utter the opening verse of the companion *Cūḷasuvajātaka* (Ja 430) rather than that of the *Mahāsuvajātaka* (Ja 429) and directs the reader to the tenth *nipāta* [Burlingame 1921]. Although the story is placed in the ninth *nipāta* in V. Fausböll's edition, Burlingame observes that it consists of ten stanzas and likely stood in the tenth *nipāta* in the Jātaka recension used by the Dhammapada commentator [Burlingame 1921]. Four modern translations in four languages are indexed on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral].
Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus records extensive Pali-internal overlap with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (21 matching passages) and three shared passages with the subsequent *Cūḷasuvajātaka* (Ja 430), particularly between segments §8.4–11.1 of Ja 429 and §9.1–11.1 of Ja 430 [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan collections [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§2.4–4.4 ↔ §4394–4400); Cūḷasuvajātaka (Ja 430) (§8.4–11.1 ↔ §9.1–11.1)
